summary: CesiumJS is an open source JavaScript library for drawing a whole-Earth globe and streaming very large geographic three-dimensional data into a web browser. Its strength is the geospatial half of the map: everything sits on the World Geodetic System 1984 ellipsoid in Earth-centred fixed coordinates, terrain and imagery and city-scale models stream by tile, and the clock is built on International Atomic Time with a leap second table rather than on browser time. Cesium created the 3D Tiles format, later approved by the Open Geospatial Consortium as a community standard, and CesiumJS is its reference implementation; it also reads glTF, the Indexed 3D Scene Layer format, and its own time-aware scene language, and it now streams captured scenes as Gaussian splats through the Khronos splatting extensions. It leaves almost everything a shared virtual world needs to others: the library contains no physics, no audio of any kind, no avatar or skeleton standard, and no multi-user networking. Two traps for a standards audience: CesiumJS has a complete position-and-orientation-on-Earth model of its own but does not read or write the Open Geospatial Consortium GeoPose encoding, which appears nowhere in the source tree; and its stereoscopic viewing mode predates the WebXR Device API and does not use it, so CesiumJS cannot drive a headset through the standard web path. All findings below were checked against the library source at version 1.144.0.

coverage.note: CesiumJS owns its whole rasterisation path: a Scene object drives a fixed, ordered list of render passes with multi-frustum depth splitting for precision at planetary range, weighted blended order-independent translucency and multisampling, in three scene modes. The pass list is internal and hardcoded, so there is no configurable render graph an outside party could target.

coverage.note: CesiumJS targets WebGL only. A WebGL 2 context is requested by default with automatic fallback to WebGL 1, though several newer subsystems now require WebGL 2. coverage.note: Position and orientation against the Earth are core, and the default orientation for an object is exactly the local east-north-up frame at its position, authored as heading, pitch and roll or as a quaternion. The trap is that CesiumJS neither reads nor writes the Open Geospatial Consortium GeoPose encoding: the word GeoPose appears nowhere in the source tree or the whole release history, and the GeoPose standard in turn never mentions Cesium. The two models line up conceptually, so a converter would be short, but nothing today exchanges poses as GeoPose documents.

coverage.note: The frame is stated unambiguously: World Geodetic System 1984 as the default ellipsoid, Earth-centred fixed Cartesian metres for all internal maths, longitude, latitude and height for authoring, plus geographic and Web Mercator map projections and a transform to the inertial celestial frame. The default ellipsoid can be changed to the Moon or Mars. Limits worth naming: only those two map projections and two matching tiling schemes exist, there is no general reprojection engine so data must arrive in a supported frame, and heights are above the ellipsoid. There is no geoid model in the library; the one exception is Indexed 3D Scene Layer data, which can be shifted to ellipsoidal height by supplying an external gravity model elevation service.

coverage.note: This is the capability CesiumJS defines rather than merely implements. Cesium created 3D Tiles, which the Open Geospatial Consortium approved as a community standard in 2018, and CesiumJS is its reference implementation, covering versions 1.0 and 1.1 including implicit tiling, subtrees, structural metadata and the styling language. Terrain streams as quantised mesh or as 3D Tiles, imagery streams from web map service, web map tile service, tile map service and template sources, and Esri Indexed 3D Scene Layer data is transcoded to glTF on load. One caveat for a standards audience: although 3D Tiles 1.1 is used in production throughout the library, the implicit tiling classes are still marked experimental in the source and are outside the project's deprecation promise.
